newsitem.title: USA: O'Leary says pleased with end of US DOE probe.
newsitem.headline: O'Leary says pleased with end of US DOE probe.

text.p: U.S. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary Wednesday said she was glad a probe into her department's travel expenses was over, and said U.S. energy industry competitors have tried to exploit the controversy.

"Our competitors are rushing to the table and laughing all the way" because her department has been deterred from efforts to promote energy exports by the travel expense controversy, O'Leary said at an aluminum industry gathering.

The department's inspector general's office this week issued a 300-page report which said there was mismanagement and shoddy bookkeeping in O'Leary's foreign travels, sometimes done to drum up business for U.S. energy companies.
But the report, which had few differences from a preliminary report released in June, did not hold any individuals responsible.
"I believe it's been 10 months; it seems like 10 years," O'Leary said. "I am pleased that the thing is done."

O'Leary took 16 overseas trips at a total cost of $4.58 million from June 1993 to December 1995, the inspector general's report said, including four trade missions to India, Pakistan, China and South Africa that cost $3.42 million.
O'Leary has testified at several congressional hearings amid complaints that she squandered taxpayers' money on extravagant overseas travels with large entourages.
"I am delighted (the report) is able to say with authority that there were no laws broken, no criminal activities," she said, complaining a "criminal taint" was raised by critics.
But the House Commerce Committee issued a scathing statement, saying the inspector general still was seeking outside opinions on possible violation of a law that bars overspending an account.
The committee complained that after almost a year, the department still could not account for $91,776 of $819,000 in expenses incurred by U.S. embassies from O'Leary's trips.
O'Leary said some of travel accounting problems stemmed from department personnel not knowing they had to deduct from their per diem expenses meals that were bought for them.
She said large sums were spent tracking down those expenses in order to recover just $3,300.

While the department has said the trade missions led to the signing of 143 business agreements with a potential monetary value of $19.7 billion, the inspector general's report said not all were firm contracts and that the department's role could not be quantified.
"The more accurate description is that the Department helped move many of these agreements forward and accelerated the signing of many of these agreements," the report said.
